title: II. Lizaveta
paragraphs: Something about this affair struck Grigory in particular, and it confirmed a very ugly, revolting suspicion. Lizaveta was a dwarfish creature, “not five foot, within a wee bit,” as many of the pious old women said of her with pity after her death. She had a broad, healthy, red face with a look of blank idiocy. Her eyes had a meek expression, but their fixed stare was unpleasant. She wandered about summer and winter alike, barefoot, wearing nothing but a hempen smock. Her hair was coarse, almost black, and curled like lamb’s wool, so that it made a sort of huge cap on her head. It was always caked with mud, with leaves, bits of stick and wood shavings stuck in it, because she always slept on the ground, in the dirt. Her father, Ilya, was a homeless, sickly drunkard who had lost everything and for many years had worked for some well-to-do tradespeople. Her mother had died long before. Ilya was spiteful and diseased, and whenever Lizaveta came back to him he beat her inhumanly. She seldom did, though, because everyone in town was ready to look after her. She was an idiot, and so especially dear to God. Ilya’s employers, and many others in the town, mostly tradespeople, tried to dress her better. For the winter they always fitted her out with high boots and a sheepskin coat. But although she let them dress her up without a struggle, she would usually walk off, preferably to the cathedral porch. There she took off everything they had given her—kerchief, sheepskin, skirt or boots—left it all lying, and walked away barefoot in her smock as before. Once a new governor of the province came through our town on a tour of inspection and saw Lizaveta. His tenderest feelings were wounded. He was told she was an idiot, but he ruled that a young woman of twenty wandering about in nothing but a smock was an offense against decency, and that it must not happen again. But the governor went on his way, and Lizaveta stayed as she was. At last her father died. As an orphan she became even more acceptable to the religious people of the town. In fact, everyone seemed to like her. Even the boys didn’t tease her, and the boys of our town, the schoolboys especially, are a mischievous lot. She would walk into strangers’ houses, and no one drove her out. Everyone was kind to her and gave her something. If she was given a copper, she took it and dropped it straight into the alms-jug at the church or the prison. If she was given a roll or a bun in the market, she handed it to the first child she met. Sometimes she would stop one of the richest ladies in town and give it to her, and the lady would be glad to accept it. She herself tasted nothing but black bread and water. When she went into an expensive shop, where costly goods or money lay about, no one watched her. They knew that even if she saw thousands of roubles left unguarded, she wouldn’t touch a farthing. She hardly ever went to church. She slept either in the church porch or in a kitchen garden, climbing over a hurdle to get in (to this day our town has many hurdles where other places have fences). At least once a week she turned up “at home,” meaning the house of her father’s old employers. In winter she went there every night and slept in the passage or the cowhouse. People were amazed that she could bear such a life, but she was used to it, and tiny as she was, she was robust. Some townspeople said she did all this out of pride, but that is hardly believable. She could scarcely speak, and only now and then gave an inarticulate grunt. How could she have been proud?

It happened on a clear, warm, moonlit night in September, many years ago. Five or six drunken revelers were walking home from the club, at what we in the provinces thought a very late hour. They took the “back-way,” which ran between the back gardens of the houses, with hurdles on both sides. It leads out onto the bridge over the long, stinking pool we were used to calling a river. Among the nettles and burdocks under the hurdle, the revelers noticed Lizaveta, asleep. They stopped to look at her, laughing, and started joking with no restraint at all and no decency. One young gentleman took it into his head to ask, as a whimsical question, whether anyone could possibly regard such an animal as a woman, and so on.... They all declared, with lofty disgust, that it was impossible. But Fyodor Pavlovitch, who was one of them, sprang forward and declared that it was by no means impossible, that there was in fact a certain piquancy in it, and so on.... It’s true that he was overplaying the buffoon at that time. He liked to push himself forward and entertain the company, ostensibly on equal terms, of course, though really he stood to them in the position of a servant. It was just after he had received the news in Petersburg of his first wife’s death. He was drinking, with crape on his hat, and behaving so shamelessly that even the most reckless among us were shocked to see him. The revelers laughed, naturally, at this unexpected opinion. One of them even began to dare him to act on it. The others rejected the idea still more emphatically, though still in the highest spirits, and at last they all went on their way. Later Fyodor Pavlovitch swore that he had gone off with them, and perhaps he had. No one knows for certain, and no one ever knew. But five or six months afterwards, the whole town was talking, with intense and sincere indignation, about Lizaveta’s condition, and trying to discover which scoundrel had wronged her. Then suddenly a terrible rumor spread across town that the scoundrel was none other than Fyodor Pavlovitch. Who started that rumor? Of the drunken band, five had left town. The one still among us was an elderly and much respected civil councilor, the father of grown-up daughters, who could hardly have spread the tale even if there had been anything in it. But rumor pointed straight at Fyodor Pavlovitch, and went on pointing at him. Of course he didn’t take it much to heart. He wouldn’t have bothered to contradict a set of tradespeople. In those days he was proud, and he talked only with his own circle of officials and nobles, whom he entertained so well.

At the time, Grigory defended his master vigorously. He picked quarrels and arguments on his behalf and managed to bring some people over to his side. “It’s the wench’s own fault,” he insisted. The culprit, he said, was Karp, a dangerous convict who had escaped from prison and whose name was well known to us, since he had been hiding in our town. The guess sounded plausible, because people remembered that Karp had been in the neighborhood that very autumn and had robbed three people. But all this talk didn’t turn popular sympathy away from the poor idiot. She was looked after better than ever. A well-to-do merchant’s widow named Kondratyev arranged to take her into her house at the end of April, meaning to keep her indoors until after the confinement. They watched her constantly, but despite their care she escaped on the very last day and made her way into Fyodor Pavlovitch’s garden. How she managed, in her state, to climb the high, strong fence stayed a mystery. Some held that someone must have lifted her over it. Others hinted at something more uncanny. The likeliest explanation is that it came about naturally: Lizaveta was used to clambering over hurdles to sleep in gardens, and somehow she had got up this fence, in spite of her condition, and then jumped down and hurt herself.

Grigory rushed to Marfa and sent her to Lizaveta, while he ran off to fetch an old midwife who lived nearby. They saved the baby, but Lizaveta died at dawn. Grigory took the baby, brought it home, sat his wife down and put it in her lap. “A child of God—an orphan is kin to everyone,” he said, “and to us more than to others. Our little lost one has sent us this child, who has come from the devil’s son and a holy innocent. Nurse him, and weep no more.”

So Marfa raised the child. He was christened Pavel, and people were quick to add Fyodorovitch (son of Fyodor). Fyodor Pavlovitch didn’t object to any of this. He thought it amusing, though he kept strongly denying that he was responsible. The townspeople were pleased that he had taken in the foundling. Later Fyodor Pavlovitch made up a surname for the boy and called him Smerdyakov, after his mother’s nickname.

So this Smerdyakov became Fyodor Pavlovitch’s second servant, and when our story begins he was living in the lodge with Grigory and Marfa. He worked as the cook. I ought to say more about this Smerdyakov, but I am ashamed to hold my readers’ attention for so long with these common menials. I will return to my story, hoping to say more about Smerdyakov as it goes on.
